Whether the defendants committed encroachment upon the plaintiffs' coal mining rights and removed coal, thereby rendering the remaining coal unworkable, based on the demarcation provided in Exhibit 3(b) and subsequent sub-leases?

Whether the purchase of castor oil by the appellants, who sold the goods to unregistered dealers who subsequently dispatched them out of the State, attracts liability for purchase tax under Section 10(b) of the Bombay Sales Tax Act?

Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the acquittal and convicting the appellant under Section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898, given that the seized articles were found in a shared almirah and the appellant was not in exclusive possession of the premises at the time of the search.

Whether the High Court recorded sufficient and compelling reasons to interfere with the trial court's acquittal, considering the trial court's finding that the prosecution failed to prove the appellant's guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

Whether the differential retirement age prescribed for employees appointed after September 1, 1956, as opposed to transferred employees, violates Article 16 of the Constitution of India by denying equality of opportunity in matters of public employment?

Whether the levy of royalty on minor minerals under the amended Rule 21 of the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules, 1966, violates Entry 50 of List II of the Constitution because the proceeds are not exclusively utilized for mineral development?
Whether the imposition of the enhanced royalty rate constitutes an unreasonable restriction on trade and commerce under Article 304(b) of the Constitution, requiring Presidential sanction?

Whether the differential royalty rates imposed on holders of quarry leases versus holders of 'Parwanas', and the exemption granted to village potters, violate the guarantee of equality under Article 14 of the Constitution?

Whether the High Court erred in applying Article 134 B of the Limitation Act, 1908, to the alienations of properties Exts. A 3, A 6, and A 12, given that the transferor and his son had ceased to perform worship or manage the temple for more than 25 years prior to the suit?

Whether the appellants acquired valid title to the disputed properties through adverse possession or prescriptive title, considering the long-standing possession and the fact that other individuals were acting as de facto managers of the temple for over 25 years?

Whether the High Court was justified in vacating the decree for arrears of rent by holding that the Rent Controller lacked jurisdiction to fix fair rent for vacant land, despite the prior final determination of ownership of the superstructure by the Court of Small Causes?

Whether the conviction of Accused 5 (Prakash) for criminal conspiracy under Section 302 read with Section 120B IPC is sustainable in law, given that the State did not appeal against his acquittal on this charge by the Sessions Judge, thereby rendering such acquittal final?

Whether the retracted confession of Accused 5 (Prakash), who was acquitted of conspiracy by the trial court and whose conviction by the High Court is under challenge, can be legally relied upon to corroborate the guilt of Accused 6 (Vinayak) for murder under Section 302 IPC?

Whether the conviction of Accused 6 (Vinayak) for murder is sustainable when the primary corroborative evidence relied upon by the High Court (the retracted confession of Accused 5) is legally infirm or inadmissible for the purpose of establishing his guilt?

Whether the Industrial Tribunal erred in law by selecting collieries, steel plants, cement factories, and aluminum companies as comparable industries for fixing minimum wages, instead of identical paper mills, given the differences in age, scale, and profitability?

Whether the Tribunal correctly upheld the exclusion of casual and badli workers from bonus payments based on the terms of the 1959 agreement?

Whether the Calcutta Thika Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 1953, which omitted Sections 28 and 29 of the 1949 Act, applies retrospectively to a suit for ejectment instituted prior to the commencement of the 1949 Act and decreed before the 1953 Amendment?

Whether the omission of Sections 28 and 29 of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949, by the 1953 Amendment rendered the civil court incompetent to try the suit or rendered the decree infructuous, thereby barring the landlord from recovering possession?

Whether the Special Area Development Authority, constituted under the Madhya Pradesh Nagar Tatha Gram Nivesh Adhiniyam, 1973, possesses the statutory competence to levy property tax on the appellants' assets under the powers conferred by Section 69(d) read with the amended Municipal Acts.

Whether Government Companies incorporated under the Companies Act, with their entire share capital owned by the Government of India, are exempt from the payment of property tax levied by local authorities under the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Acts.

Whether the State of Madhya Pradesh had the legislative competence to impose property tax on the assets of the appellants, given that the assets are mines under the control of the Union of India under Entry 54 of List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution.

Whether the licensing provisions under Section 5 of the Madras Commercial Crops Markets Act, 1933, and the associated fees constitute an unreasonable restriction on the fundamental right to carry on trade or business under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, or are they saved by Article 19(6)?

Whether the Government Order establishing a regulated market at Virudhunagar, where a private market already existed, imposes an unreasonable restriction on the appellants' fundamental rights under Article 19(1)(g) due to lack of necessity?

Whether the bye-law prohibiting the collection of 'mahimai' allowances is ultra vires Section 14 of the Act, given the contention that 'mahimai' does not fall within the statutory definition of a trade allowance?

Whether the petitioners are entitled to claim consequential benefits, including arrears of pay and notional seniority, based on the Supreme Court's judgment in Civil Appeal No. 441 of 1981, given that the 1962 circular relied upon in that judgment was superseded by subsequent government orders before the petitioners' cases were considered?

Whether the petitioners' writ petitions are maintainable or barred by the principles of laches and delay, considering they were filed approximately 17 years after the relevant period of service and after they had already been promoted in the normal course?

Whether the principle of 'no work, no pay' precludes the grant of back wages to employees who were promoted in the normal course but seek retrospective financial benefits based on a circular that was no longer operative at the time of their promotion?
Whether the High Court erred in law in holding that the appellant failed to prove that the testatrix, Lakshmamma, was in a sound and disposing state of mind at the time of executing the will?

Whether the High Court was justified in finding that the will did not represent the true intentions of the testatrix, considering the circumstances of undue influence, the appellant's role in drafting and dictating the will, and the simultaneous execution of a power of attorney?

Whether the elaborate and disputed recitals in the will regarding the testatrix's absolute title and financial transactions with her son constitute sufficient grounds to invalidate the will or cast doubt on the testatrix's free agency?

Whether the suit for restoration of possession instituted in 1974 was barred by the principle of res judicata or Order 2 Rule 2(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure due to the prior dismissal of Suit No. 157 of 1968 on technical grounds?

Whether the Civil Court had jurisdiction to entertain the suit for possession of the coconut grove, or whether such jurisdiction was ousted by the Goa, Daman & Diu Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1964, as amended by the Fifth Amendment Act of 1976?

Whether the Fifth Amendment to the Goa, Daman & Diu Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1964, which came into force during the pendency of the suit, operated retrospectively to oust the Civil Court's jurisdiction over a suit already instituted?

Whether a Judge of a High Court or the Supreme Court of India falls within the definition of 'public servant' under Section 6 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, such that they are subject to criminal prosecution for criminal misconduct under Section 5(1)(e) of the Act.

Whether the charge sheet filed by the CBI is legally valid despite the Investigating Officer's alleged failure to formally call upon the appellant to account for the disproportionate assets and record a specific finding on the satisfaction of his explanation.

Whether the exercise of power under Section 237(b) of the Companies Act, 1956, in the present circumstances, constitutes an unreasonable restriction on the right to carry on trade or business under Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, or is arbitrary and violative of Article 14.

Whether Section 46(2) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, read with Section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876, violates Article 14 of the Constitution by creating an arbitrary and unreasonable classification between different categories of tax defaulters regarding the mode of recovery and detention?

Whether the reduction of the retirement age violates Article 14 of the Constitution by being arbitrary, unreasonable, or lacking a rational nexus with the stated objectives of providing employment to youth and creating promotional avenues.

Whether the State's reliance on a policy decision to address unemployment justifies the infringement of the employees' rights under Articles 16 and 300A, or whether such a policy decision is subject to judicial review for arbitrariness and non-application of mind.
